newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont found guilty of murder but mentally ill.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont found guilty of murder but mentally ill.

text.p: John du Pont, one of the richest murder defendants in U.S. history, was found guilty on Tuesday of third degree murder but also was found to be mentally ill in the killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
The six man and six woman jury announced its verdict after deliberating for seven days.

Lawyers for du Pont, 58, had acknowledged he killed Schultz at the wrestler's home on the du Pont estate on Jan. 26, 1996, but argued du Pont suffered from paranoid schizophrenia that rendered him incapable of knowing right from wrong.
The verdict implies that du Pont killed Schultz with malice, but without the premeditation required for the first degree murder conviction sought by prosecutors.

The mental illness provision means du Pont will face the same penalty as an ordinary third degree murder verdict, but will be allowed to receive mental health treatment before serving out any remainder to his term.
Both defence lawyers and prosecutors said they were pleased with what was evidently a compromise verdict that leaves du Pont facing between five and 40 years in prison.
"I'm very pleased with this verdict, yes I am," Delaware County District Attorney Patrick Meehan told reporters.

"I think, cynically some people thought that John du Pont, who is the wealthiest murder defendant in the history of the United States ... would use his money to triumph over justice. Well, that did not occur," Meehan said.

Du Pont is a great-great grandson of E.I. du Pont, who in 1802 founded the chemical firm that bears his name and spawned one of America's largest family fortunes. John du Pont's personal wealth has been estimated at up to $250 million.

Du Pont's attorneys were disappointed the jury rejected du Pont's plea of innocent by reason of insanity, but said they were relieved the verdict recognised his mental illness and spared him the automatic life sentence of a first-degree conviction.
"I think they came to a result that we can live with," du Pont attorney Thomas Bergstrom said.
"I would like to be able to say to him (du Pont) that at some point he will go home again. And I think that this verdict gives us that opportunity," he said.
Bergstrom did not, however, rule out an appeal. He said du Pont told him "thank you" after the verdict was announced.
Schultz's widow Nancy, her eyes moist, said, "It is comforting to know that du Pont is not above the law and he must now be held responsible for David's murder."

The mental illness provision was passed following the 1981 assassination attempt against President Ronald Reagan, whose attacker, John Hinckley, was found not guilty by reason of insanity. Many critics felt the law should have stronger penalties even if the perpetrator was mentally ill.
The maximum penalty for the conviction is 20 to 40 years, with a minimum term of five years because a gun was used.
State sentencing guidelines specify a sentence of 69 months to 10 years when the killer had no prior offences, but prosecutors indicated they may argue for a stiffer sentence.
"We will certainly argue for as strong a sentence as possible," Meehan said.

Du Pont also was found guilty but mentally ill on simple assault charges for pointing a gun at a security consultant who accompanied him to the killing, but was found innocent of the same charge for pointing a gun at Schultz's widow.
His sentencing will be on April 22, at which time a hearing will also be held on his need for mental health treatment.
Testimony in the 13-day trial featured descriptions of bizarre behaviour by du Pont and delusions that he was the Dalai Lama, the last czar of Russia or the Christ child.
Du Pont was a long-time fan and patron of amateur wrestling, and established a training facility on his sprawling Foxcatcher Farm estate in suburban Philadelphia.
Schultz worked as a coach at the facility and lived with his wife and their two young children on the estate.
Schultz's shooting was followed by a 48-hour police siege of du Pont's mansion before he was captured.
